title: Business Environment
tagline: The forces around a firm, the stakeholders they affect, and the three analysis tools a manager uses to read them.

overview.intro: No business operates in a vacuum. A change in the rate of goods and services tax, a new labour judgment, a competitor’s price cut or a shift in what customers care about can each decide whether a firm thrives. The business environment is everything outside the firm that influences its working, and studying it is what separates a manager who reacts late from one who plans. This unit defines the environment and its features, separates the general forces from the specific forces, identifies the stakeholders whose interests a business must balance, and then works through the three analysis tools the syllabus expects: PESTLE for the wide picture, Porter’s five forces for the competitive pressure in an industry, and SWOT for the firm’s own position within it.

facts.label: Two layers
facts.value: The micro or specific environment of customers, suppliers and competitors; the macro or general environment of political, economic, social, technological, legal and environmental forces.

facts.label: PESTLE
facts.value: Political, Economic, Social, Technological, Legal and Environmental factors scanned one by one.

facts.label: Porter’s five forces
facts.value: Rivalry, threat of new entrants, threat of substitutes, bargaining power of buyers, bargaining power of suppliers.

facts.label: Exam weight
facts.value: Tool-based application questions and the importance of environment study recur every year.

learningOutcomes: Define the business environment and state its main features.
Distinguish general forces from specific forces and give examples of each.
Identify internal and external stakeholders and their interests.
Apply PESTLE, Porter’s five forces and SWOT to a given situation.
Explain the importance of studying the business environment.

learn.title: Meaning, features and importance of the business environment

blocks.text: The business environment refers to the totality of internal and external forces that affect the working and performance of a business. It includes the suppliers, customers and competitors the firm deals with directly, and the political, economic, social and legal conditions it merely lives within. Its features are that it is dynamic rather than static, that it is complex because many forces act at once, that it is interrelated, that it is largely outside the control of any single firm, and that it differs from sector to sector and firm to firm.

items.meaning: All internal and external forces affecting the working and results of an enterprise.
The forces close to the firm: customers, suppliers, competitors and intermediaries.
The wider forces of the economy and society that shape every industry.
Any person or group affected by, or able to affect, the decisions of the firm.

blocks.caption: Why studying the business environment matters
rows: Time to respond to a competitor’s move or a new regulation
A new market, product or technology can be spotted early
Choices are taken with the real conditions in mind
Firms seen as responsible and current attract customers and staff
Forecasts of demand, cost and interest rates anchor the plan

items.text: A rise in the goods and services tax rate changes pricing across an entire sector within weeks.
items.note: The force is macro and general, so no single firm can avoid it; only the response can differ.

items.text: A key supplier of packaging doubles its prices.
items.note: The force is micro and specific, affecting one firm’s cost structure directly.

blocks.text: The environment is usually read in two layers. The specific or micro environment consists of the forces with which the firm transacts directly: customers whose preferences decide revenue, suppliers whose reliability decides cost and continuity, competitors whose actions decide market share, and intermediaries such as wholesalers and retailers who connect the firm to the final buyer. The general or macro environment consists of the wider conditions that shape every firm in an industry at once: political stability and policy, economic growth and inflation, social demography and lifestyle, technological change, legal rules, and the natural environment.

blocks.caption: The two layers of the business environment
rows: Customers, suppliers, competitors, intermediaries, the market
Political, economic, social, technological, legal, environmental
Indirect but often decisive and unavoidable

items: A specific force can be negotiated with: a supplier’s price can be argued.
A general force has to be adapted to: a law is obeyed, not negotiated.
General forces set the boundaries within which specific forces operate.
The two interact, for example a new technology becomes a legal requirement before it becomes a customer expectation.

blocks.text: The distinction matters because it decides the response. A firm losing customers to a rival responds with marketing and product change, because the force is specific and within reach. A firm facing a recession responds with cost control and cash planning, because the force is general and outside its control.

A stakeholder is anyone who has an interest in the business and can be affected by its decisions. Internal stakeholders belong to the organisation: the owners or shareholders who supply capital and expect a return, the managers who run it, and the employees who supply labour and expect fair wages, security and satisfaction. External stakeholders stand outside it: customers who want quality at a fair price, suppliers who want timely payment, lenders who want interest and repayment, the government which wants tax and compliance, and society at large which expects the firm to act responsibly.

blocks.caption: Stakeholders and what each expects
rows: Profit, dividend and growth in share value
Goods and services for their needs

blocks.text: Conflicts between stakeholders are normal, and management is largely the art of balancing them. Higher wages reduce the profit shareholders receive; a lower price helps customers but squeezes the margin available for suppliers. The firms that last are those that recognise the claims of all groups rather than maximizing for one at the expense of the others.

items.text: A factory deciding between a dividend increase and a safety upgrade.
items.note: Shareholders favour the dividend while employees and society favour the upgrade, and the decision sets the firm’s priorities visibly.

items.text: An online retailer choosing between a cheaper supplier and one with better labour standards.
items.note: Suppliers and profit pull one way; employees of that supplier and society pull the other.

learn.title: PESTLE, Porter’s five forces and SWOT

blocks.text: Three tools carry the analytical weight of this unit. PESTLE is a scan of the wide environment: political factors such as stability and policy, economic factors such as growth, inflation and interest rates, social factors such as demography and lifestyle, technological factors such as automation and digital channels, legal factors such as employment and consumer law, and environmental factors such as climate rules and waste. PESTLE answers the question of what is happening around the industry.

Porter’s five forces narrows the lens to the competitive pressure inside an industry: the intensity of existing rivalry, the threat of new entrants, the threat of substitute products, the bargaining power of buyers, and the bargaining power of suppliers. A force is strong when the parties on that side have real choice. Many buyers with low switching costs make the buyer force powerful; a single critical supplier makes the supplier force powerful.

blocks.caption: Porter’s five forces with the question each answers
rows: How many competitors of similar size and strength are fighting for the same customers?
How easy and how expensive is it for a newcomer to enter this market?
What else could the customer use instead of our product?
How easily can customers switch to a rival and demand a lower price?
How much control do our suppliers have over the price and quality of inputs?

blocks.text: SWOT turns the lens onto the firm itself. Strengths are the internal capabilities that give an advantage, weaknesses are internal limitations, opportunities are external conditions the firm could exploit, and threats are external conditions that could damage it. The value of SWOT lies in the pairing: a strength is used to seize an opportunity, or to defend against a threat, while a weakness is repaired before a threat reaches it.

blocks.caption: SWOT applied to a neighbourhood grocery chain considering online delivery
rows: Strength: three outlets within two kilometres of most customers
Opportunity: rising demand for quick home delivery
Weakness: no ordering app and no delivery fleet
Threat: a national quick-commerce firm entering the city

keyPoints: The business environment is all internal and external forces affecting a firm’s working and results.
It is dynamic, complex, interrelated, largely outside the firm’s control and sector-specific.
The specific environment covers customers, suppliers, competitors and intermediaries.
The general environment covers political, economic, social, technological, legal and environmental forces.
A specific force can be negotiated with; a general force has to be adapted to.
Internal stakeholders are owners, managers and employees.
External stakeholders include customers, suppliers, lenders, government and society.
PESTLE scans the wide environment in six named categories.
Porter’s five forces measure competitive pressure inside an industry.
SWOT pairs internal strengths and weaknesses with external opportunities and threats.
examFocus: Application questions name a situation and ask which force or tool it belongs to; classify first, then explain why.
For PESTLE answers, give one specific factor per letter rather than one sentence covering all six.
In SWOT answers, keep the split clean: internal on one side, external on the other, and then pair them.

vocabulary.meaning: Totality of internal and external forces that affect an enterprise’s working and performance.
Forces close to the firm such as customers, suppliers, competitors and intermediaries.
Wider political, economic, social, technological, legal and environmental forces.
Person or group that affects, or is affected by, the decisions of a business.
Framework scanning political, economic, social, technological, legal and environmental factors.
Assessment of internal strengths and weaknesses against external opportunities and threats.
A different product that satisfies the same customer need.

questions.prompt: The business environment is best described as:
options: Only the competitors of a firm
All internal and external forces affecting a firm’s working and results
The physical office and its surroundings
The set of laws a business must obey
questions.answer: All internal and external forces affecting a firm’s working and results
questions.explanation: The environment covers every force, near or distant, that influences how a firm performs, not just one category of it.

questions.prompt: Which of the following belongs to the general or macro environment of a firm?
options: A supplier refusing to extend credit
A rise in the national rate of inflation
questions.answer: A rise in the national rate of inflation
questions.explanation: Inflation is an economic condition of the whole economy and affects every firm in the sector, which is the defining feature of a macro force.

questions.prompt: The bargaining power of buyers is strongest when:
options: Buyers are few and each buys in large volumes
Buyers are many, buy small quantities and can switch easily
The product is unique with no close substitute
Switching to another seller is technically difficult
questions.answer: Buyers are many, buy small quantities and can switch easily
questions.explanation: Many buyers with low switching costs and plenty of alternatives can force prices down, which is exactly what makes the buyer force strong.

questions.prompt: A firm notices that an ageing population is increasing demand for health services. Under SWOT this is:
questions.explanation: The ageing population is a condition outside the firm that it could exploit, which is the definition of an opportunity rather than an internal capability.

questions.prompt: The layer of the environment made up of customers, suppliers, competitors and intermediaries is called the __________ environment.
questions.explanation: The micro or specific environment consists of the parties the firm deals with directly, as against the macro environment of wider national and global forces.

questions.prompt: The analysis tool that scans political, economic, social, technological, legal and environmental factors is known by the initials __________ .
questions.explanation: PESTLE names the six categories of the wide environment scan, one letter for each category to be examined.

questions.prompt: State four features of the business environment.
questions.answer: Four features are: it is dynamic and keeps changing rather than remaining static; it is complex because many forces act at the same time; its parts are interrelated so a change in one produces changes elsewhere; and it is largely outside the control of an individual firm, which can only adapt to it. It also differs from sector to sector and firm to firm.
questions.explanation: Each feature needs a line of explanation, because naming a feature without saying what it means earns only half marks.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between internal and external stakeholders with examples.
questions.answer: Internal stakeholders are inside the organisation and take part in running it: owners who supply capital, managers who direct operations and employees who supply labour. External stakeholders are outside it but are affected by its decisions: customers who buy its output, suppliers who provide inputs, lenders, the government and society. The distinction rests on membership of the organisation rather than on how directly the party is affected.
questions.explanation: Both groups must be defined and supported with examples, and the basis of the distinction stated.

questions.prompt: Explain Porter’s five forces and how a manager uses them to judge the attractiveness of an industry.
questions.answer: Porter’s five forces measure the competitive pressure within an industry. Rivalry among existing firms is strong when many competitors of similar size fight for the same customers. The threat of new entrants is high when entry is cheap and easy, so incumbents must keep prices competitive. The threat of substitutes is high when customers can satisfy the same need another way, which caps the price a firm can charge. Bargaining power of buyers is high when customers buy in volume, know alternatives and can switch cheaply, and bargaining power of suppliers is high when inputs come from few sources or are unique. A manager uses the tool to judge whether an industry is attractive: where all five forces are strong, margins are squeezed and entry is unattractive; where they are weak, a firm can earn better returns.
questions.explanation: For full marks each force must be named, explained in terms of the choice available to that side, and then used to reach a judgement about attractiveness.

questions.prompt: A city bakery finds that a supermarket chain has opened three stores nearby, that flour prices have risen 20%, that customers increasingly ask for sugar-free options, and that a state regulation now requires calorie labelling. Classify each development by environment layer and by SWOT category, and recommend a response.
questions.answer: The supermarket openings are a specific environment force and a threat, since they compete directly for the same customers. The flour price rise is a specific force acting through suppliers and is also a threat because it raises cost. The demand for sugar-free products is a general social force and an opportunity, since it opens a new product line. The calorie labelling regulation is a general legal force and is neutral: it must be complied with, and compliance can itself become a strength. The response is to defend on price and convenience against the supermarkets, launch a sugar-free range to capture the opportunity, and treat accurate labelling as a mark of credibility while absorbing its small administrative cost.
questions.explanation: The question is marked on classification first and judgement second: each of the four developments must be placed in a layer and a SWOT category before any recommendation earns credit.
